title: Nellie and Pico Help the Daisy
markdown:
The ocean was a soft shimmery blue as the sun began to yawn and dip, painting the sky in mellow colours. Nellie the narwhal calf, bright spiraling tusk glittering like a sleepy star, played a gentle game of nudge and blow with Pico the puffin chick near the whispering shore. Pico was a little ball of fluff, soft and warm, wings fluttering with happy energy. They loved these quiet evenings. The water whispered secrets. The air smelled of salt and sleepy sea flowers. Calm games. Everything familiar and safe, like a cozy nest.

“Oh, Nellie,” chirped Pico, voice like tiny bells. “Look how the water sparkles. It feels like a warm blanket.” He tilted his fluffy head. Bright eyes held the softening light.

Nellie blew a little puff of bubbles. They rose and shimmered like tiny pearls, then popped softly. “It does, Pico. A very nice evening.” She loved when the world slowed, and the gentle rocking of the waves lulled her.

Then a little gust of wind, no stronger than a whisper, tumbled a tiny daisy from the grassy bank. The daisy, sunny yellow petals, was very, very sleepy. It had been a long day of basking and smiling at the sun. Its eyelids felt heavy, heavy, heavy. It tumbled, tumble, tumble, into the gentle waves, and landed with a tiny silent plop near Nellie’s nose.

Nellie blinked. “Oh dear.” She nudged the daisy with the tip of her tusk, cool and smooth. “Little daisy, you are all wet. Your flowerbed is up there, safe and warm. You need to get back before night tucks you in.” A little flutter sat in her tummy. She had never carried a daisy. Keeping something so delicate safe felt like a big task.

Pico hopped closer. “The poor little daisy.” His puffin legs wobbled. He was so small. He almost pulled back toward the familiar shore, feet wanting to be safe.

If the sleepy daisy did not reach its warm dry bed soon, its petals would close tight, and it might miss greeting the morning sun. The fading light said they should go, and quickly, but gently.

“We must help,” Nellie said, firm and kind, setting her own worry aside for a moment. “We will be very, very careful.” She lowered her head so her tusk made a gentle cradle. “To the grassy bank. It is not far. The water is shallow all the way.”

Nellie and Pico, daisy nestled on the tusk, began. The water was still soft and shimmery. Little waves nudged them. Soft slithery strands of seaweed tickled Nellie’s sides like curious fingers.

Pico puffed his little chest. “I will flutter my wings to keep it steady.” He flapped a gentle rhythm, just enough so the daisy would not rock too much. Nellie was a gentle boat. She guided them away from soft mud and away from sleepy starfish who might get in the way.

Then a long wiggly strand of seaweed caught around Nellie’s tusk and held them, just a little.

“Oh no,” chirped Pico, wings faster. “We are stuck.”

Nellie felt the tug, gentle but persistent. She tried to wiggle. The seaweed held fast, a silent green obstacle. A small fish came to look and offered no advice.

“I can peck at it,” said Pico, voice suddenly clear. He flew off the tusk, hovered, wings a blur, and pecked the thickest part. Peck, peck, peck. Nellie watched, holding still, big eyes on the determined puffin. The seaweed started to fray. Green threads broke away. Pico pecked a little more, then a little more, small beak a tiny determined tool.

With a soft snap, the strand broke free. Nellie could wiggle again. “Pico. You did it.” She nudged him with her head. “Brave and strong, even though you are small.” Pico’s fluffy chest puffed further. The size-worry melted like foam on a warm wave.

They went on, tusk sure, wings steady. A sleepy seahorse drifted by, tail curled, and nodded as if this were a usual errand. Little fish no bigger than thumbs darted, scales flashing like tiny coins. A starfish rolled over and pretended to be a stone. The grassy bank came closer, grass tips nodding. They could smell the sweet earthy scent of flowers, a perfume that promised rest. One more shallow ripple. Nellie waited so the daisy would not splash. Pico counted three flaps and then was still.

Then they were there. Nellie lowered her tusk. The sleepy daisy rested on the soft green grass, right beside its own little flowerbed, as if it had only stepped out for a moment.

Its petals drooped a little more, as if the journey had made it even more tired. A tiny cool drop sat on its yellow centre. “It is so wet,” whispered Nellie. Pico’s wings drooped too. “My feathers feel a bit cooler.” They had brought it back, and still they worried it might never feel sunny again.

Nellie looked at her damp tusk. The spiral felt less bright. Pico’s fluff was slightly slicked. “Perhaps,” Pico whispered, “we should have just left it.”

Then Nellie remembered the tumble from home, how lost it must have felt. She nudged it with her nose, a soft comforting touch. “I carried you.” Pico shook his feathers. “And I kept you steady.” They had given their best, and a little of their own comfort, to help the daisy to its green bed.

They watched a moment longer, then turned, a gentle swirl of water, back toward their own cozy places. Nellie nestled in a calm quiet cove, water lapping softly. Pico snuggled into his soft nest on the shore, sand and salt familiar. Eyes closed. Minds still a little full of the sleepy daisy. Peace beginning to settle.

Morning came. The sun, a big golden smile, peeked over the horizon and sent warm rays to the grassy bank. The little daisy, nestled in its flowerbed, slowly, slowly unfurled. Yellow bright. Face to the sun, as if it had woken from the most perfect nap.

Nellie nudged Pico. Her tusk gleamed. Pico puffed his chest, feathers fluffing in the warm sun. The daisy stretched its sunny petals wide. And everything was just right.
